questions.question_text: A drought destroys half the coffee crop while a study praises coffee's health benefits. In the coffee market:
questions.option_a: Price rises; quantity change is indeterminate
questions.option_c: Both price and quantity must rise
questions.option_d: Both price and quantity must fall
questions.explanation: Supply shifts left (drought) AND demand shifts right (study) — both push price UP, but they pull quantity in opposite directions, so quantity depends on shift magnitudes. Double-shift questions always leave one variable indeterminate.

questions.question_text: A 10% price increase causes quantity demanded to fall 25%. Total revenue will:
questions.explanation: |%ΔQ/%ΔP| = 25/10 = 2.5 > 1 → elastic. With elastic demand, the quantity loss outweighs the price gain, so revenue FALLS when price rises. The price-revenue link runs through elasticity, never through price alone.

questions.question_text: The cross-price elasticity between goods X and Y is +1.8. The goods are:
questions.explanation: Positive cross-price elasticity: Y's price rises → X's demand rises → consumers switch TO X = substitutes. Negative would mean complements (consumed together). The SIGN carries the relationship; the magnitude only measures its strength.

questions.question_text: Pizza costs $4/slice and gives you 40 utils of marginal utility; soda costs $2/can and gives 24 utils. To maximize utility you should:
questions.option_a: Buy more pizza — it has higher marginal utility
questions.option_b: Buy more soda — its marginal utility per dollar (12) exceeds pizza's (10)
questions.explanation: Compare MU per DOLLAR: pizza 40/4 = 10, soda 24/2 = 12. Reallocate toward soda until MU/P equalizes. Comparing raw marginal utilities (option A) ignores that pizza costs twice as much — the per-dollar normalization IS the consumer optimum rule.

questions.question_text: When marginal cost is below average total cost, ATC must be:
questions.explanation: The average falls whenever the marginal addition is below it — like a test score below your average dragging the average down. MC intersects ATC exactly at ATC's minimum; that geometric fact anchors half the cost-curve questions on the exam.

questions.question_text: A perfectly competitive firm is producing where P = $12 and MC = $9. To maximize profit it should:
questions.option_b: Increase output until MC rises to $12
questions.option_d: Keep output constant — it is already maximizing
questions.explanation: Each additional unit adds $12 of revenue but only ~$9 of cost — leaving profit on the table. Expand until MR (= P in perfect competition) = MC. Profit maximization is a marginal condition, not about producing 'as much as possible.'

questions.question_text: A competitive firm's price is $8, minimum ATC is $10, and minimum AVC is $6. In the short run the firm should:
questions.option_b: Operate at a loss, since P covers variable costs and contributes to fixed costs
questions.explanation: Shutdown rule: produce if P ≥ min AVC. Here $8 > $6, so operating loses LESS than shutting down (which loses all fixed costs). It can't raise price — it's a price taker. Loss-minimizing production is the concept students most often get backwards.

questions.question_text: Compared with a perfectly competitive industry, a single-price monopoly produces:
questions.option_a: More output at a lower price
questions.option_b: Less output at a higher price, creating deadweight loss
questions.option_c: The same output at a higher price
questions.option_d: More output at a higher price
questions.explanation: The monopolist restricts output to where MR = MC (MR < P because lowering price applies to all units), then charges off the demand curve. Units valued above MC go unproduced — that forgone surplus is the deadweight loss triangle.

questions.question_text: A perfectly price-discriminating monopolist differs from a single-price monopolist in that it:
questions.option_b: Produces the efficient quantity but captures all consumer surplus as profit
questions.option_d: Charges every customer the same price
questions.explanation: Charging each buyer their willingness to pay makes MR = demand, so output expands to the competitive quantity — deadweight loss vanishes, but ALL surplus goes to the producer. Efficient yet maximally inequitable: efficiency and fairness are separate questions.

questions.question_text: In long-run equilibrium, a monopolistically competitive firm earns:
questions.option_a: Positive economic profit due to differentiation
questions.option_b: Zero economic profit, with price above minimum ATC (excess capacity)
questions.option_c: Zero economic profit at minimum ATC
questions.explanation: Free entry erodes profit to zero — but the downward-sloping demand curve means tangency with ATC happens LEFT of the minimum: price exceeds min ATC and capacity sits idle. Zero profit without productive efficiency distinguishes this from perfect competition.

questions.question_text: Two firms can each set High or Low prices. Payoffs (A, B): both High (10, 10); A High/B Low (2, 12); A Low/B High (12, 2); both Low (5, 5). The Nash equilibrium is:
questions.explanation: Low is each firm's dominant strategy: whatever the rival does, Low pays more (12>10 if rival High; 5>2 if rival Low). Both end up at (5,5) even though (10,10) was available — the prisoner's dilemma. Nash = no one gains by deviating ALONE, not the best joint outcome.

questions.question_text: A firm sells output at $5 in a competitive market. Hiring a 4th worker raises output from 100 to 112 units. The marginal revenue product of that worker is:
questions.explanation: MRP = marginal product × price = 12 × $5 = $60 — hire if the wage is below $60. Option A is just MP (units, not dollars); option C is total revenue at 112 units. Factor demand runs on the marginal unit, not totals.

questions.question_text: Compared with a competitive labor market, a monopsonist employer hires:
questions.option_a: More workers at a higher wage
questions.option_b: Fewer workers at a lower wage
questions.option_c: The same number at a lower wage
questions.option_d: Fewer workers at a higher wage
questions.explanation: The sole buyer of labor faces an upward-sloping supply curve, so the marginal cost of one more hire exceeds the wage (raising wages applies to everyone). It hires where MFC = MRP, then pays the lower supply-curve wage. The monopsony graph is monopoly's mirror image in the input market.

questions.question_text: A factory's pollution harms a downstream town that isn't part of any transaction. Without intervention, the market for the factory's product will feature:
questions.option_a: Underproduction relative to the social optimum
questions.option_b: Overproduction, because the firm ignores the external cost
questions.explanation: A negative externality drives a wedge: marginal SOCIAL cost > marginal private cost. The market equilibrates on private cost → too much output. A corrective (Pigouvian) tax equal to the marginal external cost shifts supply to internalize it.

questions.question_text: National defense is a public good because it is:
questions.option_b: Non-rival and non-excludable, creating a free-rider problem
questions.explanation: The DEFINITION is the two properties: my protection doesn't reduce yours (non-rival), and no one can be excluded (non-excludable) — so private markets undersupply it because everyone waits to free-ride. 'Government provides it' is the consequence, not the definition.

questions.question_text: A binding price ceiling set below equilibrium in the apartment market causes:
questions.option_b: A shortage, with quantity demanded exceeding quantity supplied
questions.option_c: No change if landlords are profitable
questions.option_d: Higher rents in the legal market
questions.explanation: Below-equilibrium ceiling → Qd rises, Qs falls → shortage (plus non-price rationing: waitlists, black markets, quality decay). Ceilings below equilibrium bind; the mirror rule for floors (like minimum wage) is ABOVE equilibrium → surplus.

questions.question_text: A per-unit tax is imposed on a good with perfectly inelastic demand. The tax burden falls:
questions.option_b: Entirely on buyers, with no deadweight loss
questions.option_c: Equally on both, with large deadweight loss
questions.option_d: Entirely on buyers, with maximum deadweight loss
questions.explanation: With vertical demand, quantity doesn't change — buyers absorb the full price increase, and since no transactions are lost, deadweight loss is zero. Incidence follows relative elasticity (the more INELASTIC side bears more), and DWL requires a quantity change.

questions.question_text: In one hour, Ana can bake 12 loaves or make 4 pies; Ben can bake 6 loaves or make 3 pies. Who has comparative advantage in pies?
questions.option_a: Ana, because she makes more pies per hour
questions.option_b: Ben, because his opportunity cost of a pie (2 loaves) is lower than Ana's (3 loaves)
questions.option_c: Ana, because she has absolute advantage in both
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost per pie: Ana gives up 12/4 = 3 loaves; Ben gives up 6/3 = 2 loaves. Ben sacrifices less → comparative advantage in pies, despite Ana's absolute advantage in both goods. Comparative advantage is about RATIOS, never raw output.

questions.question_text: A Lorenz curve that bows farther away from the 45-degree line indicates:
questions.explanation: The 45° line is perfect equality; more bow = the bottom share of households earns a smaller share of income = more inequality = HIGHER Gini (D contradicts B). The Lorenz curve shows distribution, not the level of income.

questions.question_text: Fixed cost is $100. Producing 10 units costs $300 total. Average variable cost at 10 units is:
questions.explanation: TVC = TC − TFC = 300 − 100 = 200; AVC = 200/10 = $20. Option A is ATC (forgot to remove fixed cost); option D is total variable cost, not the average. Always strip fixed cost before averaging variable cost.
